paragraphs: This paper asks whether language models can forecast future events at a level approaching competitive human forecasters. The researchers build a system that combines information retrieval with prediction: it automatically searches for relevant material, produces forecasts, and aggregates predictions. This makes the object of study a complete forecasting process, including information gathering, rather than just a model answering a question from its stored knowledge.

To evaluate the system, the authors collect a large set of questions from competitive forecasting platforms. Their test questions were published after the language models’ knowledge cutoffs. They compare the system’s overall performance with aggregated human forecasts, making the reference point the combined predictions of competitive forecasters.

On average, the system approaches the performance of the human crowd aggregate. It exceeds that aggregate in a particular relaxed setting, so the stronger result is conditional on that setting. The findings suggest that automated language-model forecasting could provide useful predictions at scale and contribute to institutional decisions.
neurips-2024-approaching-human-level-for.tldr: A retrieval-augmented language-model system approaches competitive human crowd forecasting performance on average and surpasses it in a particular relaxed setting.

paragraphs: CA-SSLR adapts a self-supervised speech representation model by making it aware of the language and speaker in the current input. It draws language and speaker embeddings from earlier layers and uses them to condition internal representations. The approach gives the model explicit contextual information while aiming to preserve the behavior of its underlying speech representation.

The conditioning mechanism uses linear modulation: context dynamically adjusts internal representations without substantially changing the original model’s behavior. This provides a shared adaptation mechanism across speech tasks, with minimal tuning for individual tasks. Experiments report fewer trainable parameters, reduced overfitting, and improvements on tasks with limited resources or tasks unseen during development.

The reported results span language identification, speech recognition, and speaker verification. CA-SSLR achieves a 10% relative reduction in language-identification errors, a 37% improvement in speech-recognition character error rate on ML-SUPERB, and a 27% decrease in speaker-verification equal error rate on VoxCeleb-1. Together, these results support the usefulness of language and speaker conditioning across several distinct speech-processing objectives.
neurips-2024-ca-sslr-condition-aware-sel.tldr: CA-SSLR conditions speech representations on language and speaker information, improving several speech tasks with fewer trainable parameters.

paragraphs: The distributed experts problem concerns making repeated choices when the information needed to evaluate each expert is spread across servers. An expert’s overall cost must be assembled from these separate contributions. The paper studies how to make good choices while limiting the communication required to combine that information, connecting prediction quality with the cost of distributed coordination.

The authors consider both message-passing and broadcast communication, as well as different ways to aggregate costs, including sums and ℓp norms. They introduce communication-efficient protocols with near-optimal regret, a measure of the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison choice. Their guarantees also cover a strong adversary that adaptively chooses inputs.

A conditional lower bound indicates that the protocols’ communication requirements are nearly optimal under the condition supporting that bound. This places the efficiency claim alongside evidence about how much communication may be unavoidable. Implementations on HPO-B benchmarks also show empirical savings, giving practical support to the theoretical treatment across the studied settings.
neurips-2024-communication-bounds-for-th.tldr: The paper develops communication-efficient distributed expert-selection protocols with near-optimal regret and a conditional near-optimality bound on communication.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to use available pretrained models without spending heavily on labels. Data arrives one example at a time, and the learner must decide which model should predict that example. Because different models may suit different inputs, the choice depends on the example’s context. The learner must also decide when obtaining the true label is worth the labeling cost.

CAMS combines these two decisions. Its contextual selection component estimates which model is likely to work best for the current input, while its active querying component strategically requests labels. Labels therefore serve as selectively acquired feedback for future choices, rather than a requirement for every incoming example.

The authors analyze both regret and the number of label queries under adversarial and stochastic settings. Benchmark classification experiments support the approach’s practical value. On CIFAR10 and DRIFT, CAMS uses less than 10% of the labeling effort of existing methods while delivering similar or better accuracy. These findings show substantial labeling savings in those evaluations without a corresponding loss in predictive performance.
neurips-2024-contextual-active-model-sel.tldr: CAMS selects pretrained models for individual inputs and requests labels selectively, substantially reducing labeling effort in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether vision–language models retain information specific to their training images. These models learn from paired images and captions, so apparent memory could also reflect information already present in captions or general correlations in the data. The authors introduce déjà vu memorization as a way to measure retained information beyond those explanations.

Using this measure, the researchers show that a model can preserve information about individual objects in training images that cannot be inferred from the associated caption or correlations alone. They examine memorization both for individual samples and across a population. Significant memorization appears in OpenCLIP even when it is trained on as many as 50 million image-caption pairs.

The paper also evaluates text randomization as a mitigation. It considerably reduces memorization risk while having a moderate impact on downstream task performance. The result identifies a tradeoff between reducing retained training-specific information and preserving useful representations, and offers a concrete intervention alongside the proposed measurement method.
neurips-2024-deja-vu-memorization-in-vis.tldr: Déjà vu memorization measures training-image information retained by vision–language models, and text randomization substantially reduces this risk with moderate performance impact.

paragraphs: Diffusion classifiers use generative diffusion models to assign classes to inputs. Their observed resistance to adversarial attacks motivates this paper’s central question: can that resistance be supported by mathematical guarantees? The authors prove an O(1) Lipschitz bound, which constrains how much the classifier can change as its input changes, and establish certified robustness.

To obtain tighter certificates, they extend the classifiers to operate on Gaussian-corrupted data. They derive evidence lower bounds for the relevant distributions, use those bounds to approximate likelihoods, and apply Bayes’ theorem to calculate class probabilities. The resulting Noised Diffusion Classifiers connect noise-aware generative modeling with stronger robustness certification.

On CIFAR-10, the reported certified robustness exceeds 80% for adversarial perturbations with ℓ2 norms below 0.25 and 70% for norms below 0.5. These results use one off-the-shelf diffusion model and no additional data. The certificates concern the specified perturbation sizes, providing a stronger form of evidence within those bounds than success against a particular collection of attacks alone.
neurips-2024-diffusion-models-are-certif.tldr: The paper proves robustness guarantees for diffusion classifiers and tightens certification through classifiers designed for Gaussian-corrupted inputs.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains decision-making policies from previously collected data. Diffusion policies offer an expressive way to represent actions, but generating actions through repeated denoising slows training and deployment. This paper introduces Diffusion Trusted Q-Learning, or DTQL, to retain the benefits of a diffusion policy while using a practical policy that produces actions in one step.

DTQL assigns separate jobs to its two policies. The diffusion policy learns to imitate the dataset’s behavior. A diffusion trust region loss then connects it to the one-step policy, allowing that policy to seek promising modes within a region defined by the diffusion policy. This connection removes the need for iterative denoising sampling during both training and inference.

The authors compare DTQL’s behavior with KL-based distillation methods in two-dimensional bandit settings and gym tasks. They also report that DTQL outperforms other methods on most D4RL benchmark tasks while improving training and inference efficiency. The results support using the diffusion model to define a useful region for learning a fast action policy.
neurips-2024-diffusion-policies-creating.tldr: DTQL uses a diffusion policy to guide a one-step policy, avoiding iterative action sampling while achieving strong offline reinforcement-learning results.

paragraphs: EMGBench evaluates how well electromyography classifiers handle inputs that differ from their training data. These classifiers use EMG signals to predict a person’s intended gesture, supporting wearable control interfaces for computers, prosthetics, and mobile manipulator robots. Performance under changing data distributions matters because a usable interface needs to remain effective beyond the conditions represented during training.

The benchmark organizes evaluation around two tasks: classification across different subjects and adaptation using train-test splits for time-series data. It brings together nine datasets and introduces a new dataset collected with an easy-to-wear, high-density EMG device. This collection gives researchers a shared basis for examining both generalization and adaptation.

The contribution addresses a comparison problem in EMG research: without shared open-source benchmarks, accuracy figures from separate papers are difficult to compare. EMGBench supplies a common evaluation resource focused on practically relevant distribution changes. Its central result is the benchmark and new dataset, enabling more consistent assessment of algorithms intended for robust, adaptable control interfaces.
neurips-2024-emgbench-benchmarking-out-o.tldr: EMGBench brings together nine datasets to evaluate EMG gesture classifiers on cross-subject generalization and time-series adaptation.

paragraphs: Gaussian Graph Network improves how multiple images are combined into a Gaussian representation of a scene. Existing feed-forward approaches predict Gaussians aligned with image pixels and combine them across views. The paper argues that simply collecting these predictions fails to fully account for relationships between views, producing visual artifacts and unnecessary memory costs.

The proposed network constructs graphs connecting groups of Gaussians from different images. It adapts graph operations to Gaussian representations so that each Gaussian can receive and combine information from connected groups. A Gaussian pooling layer then aggregates groups into a more compact representation. Together, these mechanisms make cross-view relationships part of the learned scene representation.

Experiments on RealEstate10K and ACID demonstrate the method’s efficiency and ability to generalize across scenes. Compared with the evaluated state-of-the-art approaches, GGN produces better image quality using fewer Gaussians and renders faster. These findings show that explicitly combining related Gaussian information can improve both representation compactness and the quality of synthesized views.
neurips-2024-gaussian-graph-network-lear.tldr: Gaussian Graph Network connects and pools Gaussians across image views, improving rendering quality and speed while using fewer Gaussians.

paragraphs: GDeR addresses the cost of training graph neural networks on large datasets while accounting for imbalance and noise. Removing training examples can reduce computation, but an unrepresentative retained subset can damage accuracy. The paper seeks a pruning method that combines efficiency with representative, balanced, and unbiased selection.

Its approach dynamically updates the subset used for training through trainable prototypes. It first constructs a graph embedding space on a hypersphere and samples training subsets from that space. Because the training collection changes during the process, the method uses soft, dynamic pruning to pursue the paper’s combined efficiency and robustness objectives.

Across four datasets and three graph neural network backbones, GDeR matches or exceeds full-dataset performance with 30–50% fewer training samples. It reports a training speedup of up to 2.81 times without performance loss. Against state-of-the-art pruning methods, reported improvements range from 0.3–4.3% in imbalanced training and 3.6–7.8% in noisy training. These results support the approach across the evaluated data conditions and model backbones.
neurips-2024-gder-safeguarding-efficienc.tldr: GDeR dynamically selects graph training subsets using prototypes, reducing training costs while improving results under imbalance and noise.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine learning across users whose data may differ substantially. Knowledge distillation can improve global model performance under this heterogeneity, but the paper identifies a security tradeoff: distillation-based methods can suffer larger accuracy losses under model poisoning attacks. The authors call this effect attack amplification and investigate it through a case study and empirical evidence.

HYDRA-FL responds with a hybrid distillation strategy. It transfers part of the distillation loss to a shallow layer using an auxiliary classifier. This changes where the distillation objective acts within the model, with the aim of reducing the impact of attacks while preserving the performance benefits that motivated distillation.

The authors present HYDRA-FL as a general framework and adapt it to FedNTD and MOON. In these two case studies, it outperforms baselines under attacks while maintaining comparable performance in benign conditions. The evidence supports the proposed modification in the tested algorithms and connects an observed vulnerability to a concrete change in how distillation is applied.
neurips-2024-hydra-fl-hybrid-knowledge-d.tldr: HYDRA-FL redirects part of knowledge distillation to a shallow classifier, reducing poisoning-related performance losses in two federated-learning case studies.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems affect several groups at once: the platform operating the service, the sellers or items being recommended, and the users receiving recommendations. These groups have different objectives, so improving one objective can complicate the others. This paper develops a framework for explicitly balancing platform revenue with fairness for both items and users.

The framework, called Problem (FAIR), expresses the recommendation problem through constrained optimization. Fairness requirements become part of the decision problem, allowing the balance among stakeholder interests to be adjusted. The authors then study an online setting, where the system must make recommendations while learning from uncertain data as it arrives.

Their algorithm, FORM, carries out learning and fair recommendation together and comes with a low-regret analysis. This addresses the tension between acquiring useful information and meeting current recommendation objectives. Theoretical results and a numerical case study using real-world data support the framework’s ability to maintain platform revenue while achieving desired fairness levels for items and users in the studied setting.
neurips-2024-interpolating-item-and-user.tldr: FAIR and its online algorithm FORM balance platform revenue with adjustable fairness requirements for both recommendation items and users.

paragraphs: This paper simplifies learning successor features directly from visual observations in reinforcement learning. Successor features offer a possible way to address forgetting and interference when environments change. However, standard pixel-based learning approaches can produce collapsed representations that fail to distinguish meaningful differences in observations. More recent alternatives avoid collapse at the cost of complicated objectives and multiple learning stages.

The proposed method combines a temporal-difference loss with a reward prediction loss. The authors describe these two objectives as capturing the basic mathematical definition of successor features. This provides a streamlined learning procedure that operates directly on pixels and does not require pretraining, reducing the machinery needed to learn useful representations.

Experiments cover two-dimensional Minigrid mazes and three-dimensional Miniworld mazes, under both single-task and continual-learning scenarios. The method matches or outperforms existing successor-feature approaches and can reach higher performance in less time. These results support the effectiveness of the simpler objective in the evaluated environments, including settings where learning must continue across changing tasks.
neurips-2024-learning-successor-features.tldr: A combination of temporal-difference and reward prediction losses learns successor features from pixels efficiently, without pretraining.

paragraphs: Large vision–language models commonly represent every image with a fixed number of visual tokens, limiting their flexibility when computation budgets change. Matryoshka Query Transformer lets a single trained model use any number of visual tokens up to a chosen maximum. This makes the amount of image information passed to the language model adjustable at inference time.

MQT compresses visual embeddings through a query transformer with a maximum number of latent queries. During training, it randomly chooses a smaller count and uses only that prefix of queries. Repeating this process trains nested token sets, allowing one model to serve different token budgets with similar or better performance than separately trained models.

MQT-LLaVA matches LLaVA-1.5 across 11 benchmarks using at most 256 tokens instead of 576. At 16 tokens, it uses eight times fewer TFLOPs with a 2.4-point MMBench decline. With two tokens, reported performance drops are 3% on ScienceQA and 6% on MMMU. The results demonstrate a task-dependent tradeoff between computation and accuracy.
neurips-2024-matryoshka-query-transforme.tldr: MQT trains one vision–language model to work with adjustable visual-token counts, enabling substantial computational savings with task-dependent performance tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Optimus-1 tackles tasks that require an agent to sustain useful behavior over many steps in an open world. The authors attribute existing agents’ difficulties partly to insufficient world knowledge and multimodal experience. Their solution gives an agent two complementary forms of memory: structured knowledge about the world and summarized experience from its previous activity.

The knowledge component organizes information into a hierarchical directed graph, supporting explicit representation and learning of world knowledge. The experience component stores abstracted multimodal histories that can serve as references for in-context learning. Optimus-1 combines these memories with a planner guided by knowledge and a reflector guided by experience, supporting planning and reflection during Minecraft tasks.

On challenging long-horizon benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over existing agents and near-human performance on many tasks. They also test different multimodal language-model backbones and report strong generalization with the memory module, including results above the GPT-4V baseline on many tasks. These findings support combining structured knowledge and past experience for extended agent behavior.
neurips-2024-optimus-1-hybrid-multimodal.tldr: Optimus-1 combines structured world knowledge and summarized multimodal experience to improve planning and reflection on long-horizon Minecraft tasks.

paragraphs: When observations are noisy curves, variation along both axes can become entangled with measurement error. This makes recovering a population-level reference function and its uncertainty difficult, and the sources of variation cannot generally be separated. The paper instead asks which geometric properties of that function can be recovered reliably within a probabilistic model.

The authors show that the size-and-shape of a square-integrable reference function can be recovered under their Bayesian functional mixed model. Here, size-and-shape means a property unchanged by a specified family of joint transformations of the two axes. The model describes these transformations as rotations in a Hilbert space and uses random transformations to capture individual differences that preserve this property.

A separate random linear term and measurement error represent changes that alter size-and-shape. Priors regularize the transformations, whose posterior summaries can be interpreted as data-driven rotations of a fixed orthonormal basis. Numerical experiments demonstrate usefulness and superiority over the compared state-of-the-art approach. The recovery claim concerns this invariant geometric property under the proposed model.
neurips-2024-probabilistic-size-and-shap.tldr: A Bayesian functional mixed model recovers an invariant size-and-shape property of a reference curve despite confounded variation and measurement noise.

paragraphs: Applying statistical risk control to generated language requires a usable definition of correctness. This paper uses textual entailment, judging correctness through whether the relevant text supports a generated sequence. It proposes two selective generation algorithms with theoretical control of the false discovery rate defined relative to that entailment relation, called FDR-E.

The supervised algorithm, SGenSup, learns from human-annotated entailment labels. To reduce dependence on costly annotation, SGenSemi also uses unlabeled data with pseudo-labels produced through an entailment set function learned using conformal prediction. The semi-supervised method further supports a broader family of neural selection functions and selection of an optimal function class among supplied candidates.

Experiments on both open-source and closed-source generative language models show that the methods achieve desired FDR-E levels with selection efficiency comparable to baselines. This supports controlled selection of generated outputs while retaining a useful amount of output. The guarantee is specifically about errors measured through textual entailment, which is the paper’s chosen basis for making generation risk mathematically controllable.
neurips-2024-selective-generation-for-co.tldr: Two selective generation methods provide theoretical false-discovery control measured through textual entailment, with supervised and semi-supervised training options.

paragraphs: SETLEXSEM tests whether language models perform set operations consistently when the symbols in the sets change. Finite sets can contain numbers, words, or other arbitrary members, making them useful for separating an operation’s rules from the surface form and meaning of its inputs. The benchmark systematically varies both the requested operation and how set members are constructed.

The authors evaluate seven language models and find poor robustness to changes in operations and operands. Their sampling framework varies lexical and semantic properties, exposing distinctive failures on easily constructed semantic groupings described as deceptive sets. These results show that a model’s performance on an algorithmic task can depend on the particular content used to express it.

The paper also examines the difficulty of separately measuring effects from member frequency and length, and presents an analysis that treats them independently. This matters for interpreting which input properties accompany performance changes. The resulting benchmark provides a controlled way to probe instruction following and algorithmic consistency across variations that should leave the underlying set rules intact.
neurips-2024-setlexsem-challenge-using-s.tldr: SETLEXSEM reveals that seven language models perform set operations inconsistently when the wording, meaning, and construction of set members change.

paragraphs: SpeechAlign studies how preference optimization can improve speech generated by neural codec language models. The paper first analyzes a distribution gap between training and inference and connects that mismatch to degraded performance. Its central proposal is to use an iterative preference-based learning process to reduce the gap and better align speech output with human preferences.

Each iteration constructs a preference dataset contrasting golden codec tokens with synthetic tokens. The model then undergoes preference optimization using these contrasts. Repeating dataset construction and optimization creates a self-improvement cycle, with the goal of progressively strengthening the speech model through successive rounds of training.

Both subjective and objective evaluations support the claim that SpeechAlign can bridge the distribution gap and enable continued improvement. The authors also report strong generalization and effectiveness for smaller models. Together, these findings suggest that preference optimization can serve as a repeated improvement mechanism for speech generation, connecting the training procedure more closely to the kinds of outputs the model produces during use.
neurips-2024-speechalign-aligning-speech.tldr: SpeechAlign iteratively optimizes preferences over reference and synthetic codec tokens to improve speech generation and reduce training–inference mismatch.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an explicit three-dimensional representation that can support several kinds of video processing. Existing approaches can struggle with complex motion when they lack 3D structure, while implicit 3D representations can be awkward to manipulate. The proposed video Gaussian representation provides explicit elements for representing both a video’s appearance and its motion.

Appearance is modeled by Gaussians in a shared canonical 3D space, and each Gaussian is associated with three-dimensional motion. Learning this representation from video is an ill-posed problem, so the method uses optical-flow and depth priors obtained from foundation models to regularize learning. These priors help constrain the representation inferred from the observed video.

The authors demonstrate applications in tracking, consistent video depth and feature refinement, editing motion and appearance, and generating stereoscopic video. The breadth of these applications supports the representation’s versatility. Its main contribution is a common, explicit structure that connects appearance with motion and can be used across several processing and manipulation tasks.
neurips-2024-splatter-a-video-video-gaus.tldr: An explicit video representation built from moving 3D Gaussians supports tracking, depth refinement, editing, and stereoscopic video generation.

paragraphs: SWE-agent investigates how software interfaces affect language-model agents performing programming tasks. The authors treat agents as a category of software users with their own capabilities and needs. This motivates designing an interface around the actions an agent must perform when solving a software engineering problem.

The resulting system gives agents a custom interface for creating and editing code files, navigating repositories, and running tests or other programs. These capabilities support autonomous interaction with a working software environment. The paper reports that the interface substantially improves the agent’s ability to carry out these activities and examines how interface choices influence behavior and performance.

On SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix, SWE-agent achieves reported state-of-the-art pass@1 rates of 12.5% and 87.7%, respectively. These figures describe success on a first attempt and substantially exceed the previous results from non-interactive language models. The findings establish interface design as a consequential component of the evaluated software-engineering system, alongside the language model that uses it.
neurips-2024-swe-agent-agent-computer-in.tldr: SWE-agent uses a custom computer interface to improve language-model agents’ repository navigation, code editing, test execution, and software-task performance.

paragraphs: TFGDA addresses transferring knowledge from a graph with few labels to unlabeled nodes in a target graph. Many approaches align feature distributions across domains, but the authors argue that this overlooks useful information in graph structure. Their framework combines structural alignment, feature alignment, and clustering to support transfer when labeled examples are scarce.

Its STSA component encodes topological information into a latent representation, helping the model learn transferable features from how graph elements are connected. The SDA component reduces differences between domains on a spherical representation space to stabilize feature alignment. A third component, RNC, guides discriminative clustering of unlabeled nodes to address overfitting associated with limited labels.

These components tackle complementary parts of the transfer problem: structural information, differences in feature distributions, and the shortage of direct supervision. Experiments on several benchmarks report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support incorporating graph topology into domain adaptation together with feature alignment and guidance from unlabeled-node clustering.
neurips-2024-tfgda-exploring-topology-an.tldr: TFGDA combines graph-structure alignment, spherical feature alignment, and unlabeled-node clustering to improve transfer between graphs with scarce labels.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detection depends on what a dataset considers abnormal, and those criteria can differ across domains. A model trained and evaluated within one dataset may therefore transfer poorly elsewhere. This paper introduces multi-domain video anomaly detection, training a general model on several datasets simultaneously and studying the conflicts that arise between their definitions of abnormality.

The authors experimentally observe that these abnormality conflicts impede learning and generalization. They define two objectives: distinguishing broadly normal from abnormal events across domains, and recognizing ambiguous conflicts. To study both, they introduce a benchmark, baseline methods, and evaluation protocols rather than treating all datasets as sharing a single uncomplicated notion of abnormal behavior.

The proposed baseline combines Null(Angular)-Multiple Instance Learning with an Abnormal Conflict classifier. Experiments use six video anomaly detection datasets and four evaluation protocols. They reveal the conflicts and show that the baseline handles them effectively, with robustness and adaptability across multiple domains. The contribution makes conflicting anomaly criteria an explicit part of both learning and evaluation.
neurips-2024-towards-multi-domain-learni.tldr: A multi-domain video anomaly benchmark and baseline explicitly address conflicts in what different datasets classify as abnormal.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural-network training through interactions among input variables. Earlier theoretical work established that, for a given input, a small collection of such interactions can faithfully represent a network’s detailed inference logic. This makes interactions a way to describe the patterns underlying a prediction and to investigate how those patterns develop during training.

Prior observations found two distinct phases in how networks learn interactions of different complexities, linking that progression to the transition from underfitting to overfitting. The present paper mathematically proves the two-phase dynamics. Its contribution is a theoretical mechanism connecting changes in learned interactions with changes in generalization over the training process.

Experiments across different neural networks and tasks show that the theory predicts the observed interaction dynamics well. This empirical agreement supports using interactions to study how a network’s inference patterns evolve. The explanation operates at the level of interaction learning, bringing a mathematical account to a training phenomenon that had previously been observed experimentally.
neurips-2024-towards-the-dynamics-of-a-d.tldr: The paper proves two-phase dynamics in neural networks’ learning of input interactions and connects those dynamics to changing generalization during training.

paragraphs: WebUOT-1M expands the data available for tracking objects in underwater video. The benchmark contains 1.1 million frames across 1,500 clips drawn from 408 target categories. Its bounding boxes are manually annotated and verified, and its varied underwater environments address limitations in the scale and diversity of earlier datasets.

The dataset also includes language prompts for video sequences, supporting uses such as vision-language tracking. Alongside the benchmark, the authors address the poor transfer of trackers designed for open-air conditions to underwater scenes. Their framework uses omni-knowledge distillation to train a student Transformer, transferring knowledge from the open-air domain to an underwater tracking model.

Results on existing underwater datasets and WebUOT-1M demonstrate effective knowledge transfer through the proposed framework. The authors additionally evaluate 30 deep trackers on the new benchmark. Together, the dataset and experiments provide a broader basis for comparing underwater tracking methods, while the distillation approach offers a tested way to reuse knowledge developed in a different visual domain.
neurips-2024-webuot-1m-advancing-deep-un.tldr: WebUOT-1M supplies a large, diverse underwater tracking benchmark and a distillation framework for transferring knowledge from open-air trackers.
